findings.title: The fixture-drift gate is PG-VERSION-SENSITIVE, and CI (pg14) differs from any pg17+ machine a lane might build on
findings.evidence: The local scratch cluster is PostgreSQL 18.3. `pnpm --filter @workspace/db run test:fixture:drift` failed with exactly one differing line: `determined_by_instrument text NOT NULL` (fixture) vs `determined_by_instrument text CONSTRAINT smart_file_absence_determinat_determined_by_instrument_not_null NOT NULL` (pg18 dump). CI runs `pgvector/pgvector:pg14` (.github/workflows/pr-checks.yml:42), and the checked-in fixture contains ZERO named-not-null constraints across its 4229 lines, confirming it was captured on a pre-17 server.
findings.rootCause: PG17+ tracks NOT NULL as named catalog constraints and pg_dump emits the name only when the auto-generated name was TRUNCATED at the 63-char identifier limit. `smart_file_absence_determinations_determined_by_instrument_not_null` is 67 characters, so it truncated and got emitted; every other column's name fit and stayed implicit.
findings.whyItMatters: A lane building on a modern local Postgres would either (a) commit a fixture that CI's pg14 rejects as drift, or (b) hand-normalize the line and ship a fixture whose correctness rests on unverifiable reasoning about a server version it cannot run. Both are bad, and the second is worse because it looks green.
findings.howItWasResolved: Not by hand-tuning the fixture. The column was RENAMED so no identifier can truncate on any version — see F-A2-CP2-2. After the rename the drift gate prints `Schema fixture matches live DB.` on pg18, and because nothing truncates, pg14 produces byte-identical output.
findings.durableRecommendation: Worth a backlog item: the drift script could pin or report the server version, so a future mismatch reports itself as version skew rather than as a schema error. Not fixed in this lane (out of scope, and it is a shared-tooling change).

findings.title: In-scope change recorded rather than made silently: the column was renamed determined_by_instrument -> determined_by
findings.what: The determination table's attribution column is `determined_by`, not the `determined_by_instrument` name CP1 designed (which mirrored the spine's `verified_by_instrument`).
findings.why: Purely to keep the longest auto-generated constraint name under Postgres's 63-character identifier limit, which removes the version-dependent dump behavior in F-A2-CP2-1 at the root. It is a naming change with no semantic effect: the column is still NOT NULL, still check-constrained non-empty, and still carries exactly what did the determining.
findings.recordedBecause: CP1 declared the other name. A design changed during the build is a deviation from the frozen record and gets stated, not quietly absorbed — even when the reason is mundane.
findings.verification: After the rename: full lib build exit 0, api-server typecheck exit 0, 47/47 contract tests, 37/37 integration tests, drift gate `Schema fixture matches live DB.` exit 0. Zero references to the old name remain in source (`grep -rn` returns only stale `lib/db/dist/` build output, which is generated and gitignored).

findings.title: The store's read path now PARSES the entityId, which surfaced a state the CP1 taxonomy had not assigned
findings.what: A malformed entityId (one that does not match the declared shape) cannot be a `not-sought` absence, because `not-sought` carries a jurisdictionFips and docSlug that a malformed id cannot supply. It is reported as `lookup-failed` with a basis naming the malformation.
findings.whyItMatters: This is the reconstruction trap the family exists to prevent, arriving from the other direction: a malformed id matches zero rows, and without this branch it would have read as an honest `not-sought` — an absence claim derived from a broken request. Reporting it as a failed lookup says the true thing, which is that no lookup happened.
findings.disposition: Handled in the store and covered by the type. It did not require a sixth status, which is the outcome I wanted to confirm before adding one.

adversarialReviewAtCP2.q1_isTheAbsenceActuallyUnforgeable: Attacked the central claim by asking what it would take to get `absent-verified` out of the store without a deliberate write. Traced every path: readDocument reads the verdict from a determination row and never constructs one; recordAbsenceDetermination is the only writer and validates basis before writing; and the DB check constraint refuses an uncited row even from raw SQL. The integration test `has NO determination row for a document nobody looked for` is the direct probe. I could not construct a forging path.
adversarialReviewAtCP2.q2_didITestTheTestsOrJustWriteThem: Three mutation probes (M1, M2, M3), each observed FAILING on a real exit code before being reverted. Without M1 in particular, the claim 'the type enforces it' would have been an assertion about my own code that nobody had checked.
adversarialReviewAtCP2.q3_isTheFifthStatusEarningItsPlace: held-version-absent was the status I was most prepared to drop. It survives because the conflation is live in the merged G-14 code (two return-null sites, lines 307 and 322) and because the correct RENDERING of the two differs: one says we lack a document, the other says we have it and can offer versions 1..N. Also confirmed nothing produces a sixth status (see F-A2-CP2-3).
adversarialReviewAtCP2.q4_whatDidINotProve: Stated plainly rather than left implied: nothing here is deployed, nothing is served to a customer, and no migration is applied to any deployment database. The freshness probe is on the STORE read path, not a serving revision, so DEV_PROCESS 4.4 is NOT satisfied and G-53 still owes the re-probe. The local Postgres is pg18 while CI is pg14; CI is authoritative and its conclusion string is the merge gate.
